newsitem.title: CHINA: China closes 26 pirate CD lines in 1996.
newsitem.headline: China closes 26 pirate CD lines in 1996.

text.p: China closed 26 production lines producing pirate compact discs in 1996 and would push ahead this year with a fiercer crackdown on copyright thieves, officials said on Thursday.

The price of legal compact discs (CDs) had declined in 1996, the Xinhua news agency quoted Shen Rengan, deputy director of the State Copyright Administration, as saying, meaning smaller profits for pirates.
But no stunning news in the area of copyrights was expected this year after authorities seized 26 underground production lines producing pirate CDs last year, he said.
"There is still a lot of work to do in 1997, however," he was quoted as saying.
China would revise its six-year-old copyright law to meet changing needs, particularly with the development of the electronic information era, he said.
He welcomed the easing of pressure that had resulted from an accord with the United States last year on curbing piracy of intellectual property rights.

U.S. officials said last month there were indications that China was doing a better job of enforcing the Sino-U.S. copyright accord that averted a trade war last June, citing plant closures and tougher controls on importing illegal equipment.

Washington has long accused Beijing of doing too little to curb the lucrative pirating of U.S. intellectual property rights. Beijing says it has moved faster than any other nation to crack down on the underground industry.
Most illegal CDs seized last year were pirate products, Xinhua quoted Wang Huapeng, head of the administration's Copyright Department, as saying.
"As for illegal products confiscated by the authorities, only 10 percent were pornographic materials," he was quoted as saying. "The rest were mainly pirated ones."
A lot of cases would be handled this year, and a copyright protection centre would be created, Wang said, adding that the administration would oversee the work of foreign copyright agencies in China.
China would develop a new regulation on increasing writers' profits this year, he said.
Officials said their improvements were not the result of outside pressure but domestic policy priorities.
